n: Under the law, a man who divorced his wife couldn’t remarry her after she married someone else. Judah has been unfaithful with many “lovers” (idols)—yet amazingly God still says, “Return to Me.” His mercy goes beyond what the law required.

f.w: If a man put away his wife

n: Look at the hilltop shrines—there’s no place you haven’t been unfaithful. You sat by the roadside waiting for lovers like a desert nomad waiting to ambush travelers.

f.g: Hilltop shrines where idols were worshipped.

f.w: as the Arabian in the wilderness
f.g: Like a desert raider lying in wait.

n: That’s why the rains were held back. Yet you have the brazen face of a prostitute and refuse to be ashamed.

f.w: there hath been no latter rain
f.g: The spring rains (March–April) that ripen crops.

n: Haven’t you just been calling Me, “My Father, the companion of my youth”? Their words were affectionate, but their lives didn’t match.

f.g: The close companion or husband of my youth.

n: “Surely He won’t stay angry forever!” they say—while doing all the evil they can. Easy talk about God’s mercy without repentance.

f.w: Will he reserve his anger for ever?

n: A new message from Josiah’s reign. God asks Jeremiah if he has noticed what “faithless Israel”—the northern kingdom—did on every hill and under every tree.

f.g: Faithless or turning-away Israel—the northern kingdom, conquered by Assyria in 722 BC.

n: God waited for Israel to return, but she didn’t, and her treacherous sister Judah watched it all.
God gave northern Israel a “certificate of divorce”—exile by Assyria—yet Judah wasn’t afraid and did the same thing.
Treating unfaithfulness lightly, Israel polluted the land, committing “adultery” with stone and wooden idols.

f.g: Stone pillars and wooden poles used in idol worship.

n: Even after all this, Judah returned to God only in pretense, not with her whole heart. Josiah’s reforms changed outward worship, but many hearts stayed the same.
Surprisingly, faithless Israel looks more righteous than treacherous Judah, because Judah had Israel’s example and still didn’t learn.
Jeremiah is sent to call toward the north, where Israel’s exiles were scattered: “Return, faithless Israel. I won’t frown on you, for I am merciful and won’t stay angry forever.”
Just admit your sin—that you rebelled, gave your love to foreign gods, and didn’t obey. Acknowledging sin is the doorway to forgiveness.

Return, faithless children, for I am your husband. I will take you one from a city and two from a family and bring you to Zion. Latter-day Saints often apply this to the latter-day gathering—converts gathered a few at a time.

f.w: one of a city, and two of a family

n: God will give them shepherds after His own heart who will feed them with knowledge and understanding—faithful leaders, unlike the self-serving ones of Jeremiah’s day.

When the people multiply, they won’t even talk about the ark of the covenant anymore, or miss it or rebuild it. God’s presence will no longer be tied to one sacred box. The ark seems to have disappeared around the Babylonian conquest.
Instead, all of Jerusalem will be called the throne of the Lord, and all nations will gather there in His name, no longer following their stubborn, evil hearts.

f.w: the imagination of their evil heart
f.g: Stubbornness of heart—a favorite phrase of Jeremiah.

n: Judah and Israel—divided since Solomon’s death—will walk together again, returning from the north to the promised land. A prophecy of reunion among the tribes.

f.w: the house of Judah shall walk with the house of Israel
out of the land of the north

n: God says: I longed to treat you as My own children, giving you the loveliest inheritance on earth, and I hoped you would call Me “My Father” and never turn away.

f.w: Thou shalt call me, My father

n: But like a wife who betrays her husband, Israel has been unfaithful to God.
Weeping is heard on the hilltops—the very places of idolatry—as Israel cries, realizing they twisted their path and forgot the Lord.
God calls, “Return, and I will heal your faithlessness.” The people respond: “Here we come, for You are the Lord our God.” A model of repentance: God invites, and people answer.
The people confess: the noisy rites on the hills were a delusion. Salvation is truly found only in the Lord our God.

f.w: truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel

n: “The shameful thing” (often a nickname for Baal) has devoured everything our ancestors worked for—even our sons and daughters, possibly referring to child sacrifice.

f.g: Hebrew boshet, a mocking substitute for the name Baal.

n: Let us lie down in our shame and be covered with disgrace, for we and our ancestors have sinned and not obeyed. Honest, complete confession.

f.w: we have sinned against the LORD our God
